items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: Because if you don't have a Harry Carney or a Johnny Hodges Gonzalves in there and Paul Gonzales and all that, it doesn't mean anything.

ctx.x: And Strayhorn told me that Duke taught him extremes. Like he would put Carney's (PHONETIC) -- the baritone, normally everybody puts the baritone on the bottom, but he would put Paul on the bottom and put Carney up in the middle of the section and get a completely different sound. Put him in, you know, different, odd registers. You know? And those guys had great sounds. Oh, they had -- they all had great tones, you know? And I may have said this before -- I think I did say it before -- I had written this thing for…

And she took the arrangement to some other orchestra and I heard it and I said, "Ella take that out of the book, because it doesn't sound good. It sounds like, you know, it sounds very like what we call vanilla." Just nothing, you know. Because if you don't have a Harry Carney or a Johnny Hodges Gonzalves in there and Paul Gonzales and all that, it doesn't mean anything. The personalities are not there. And --
Well, Duke definitely wrote for the sound of the individual.
